For it is said that, for offence against God, Nabuchodonosor was turned to madness and for seven years lived among the beasts, on herbs and roots, and afterwards, restored to his kingdom, praised and glorified the King of heaven, because “all his works are true, and his ways judgments, and them that walk in pride he is able to abase.” But because some wish to understand by Nabuchodonosor the opposing power, of which it is said: “I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven.” And in the Apocalypse: “The dragon, falling to the earth, draws with him the third part of the stars.” And Isaias: “How art thou fallen, Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?” They assert that it could not have happened that a man nourished in delights should live seven years on hay, and be so long among the beasts without the tearing of his body. And they ask by way of objection: if another succeeded him, whose folly was it, if he yielded to him the empire which he held so greatly; or how the empire was kept for him for so long a time, and he was without a king, especially since the histories of the Chaldeans contain nothing of the kind, nor could those who wrote of lesser things have passed over these in silence. All these things they urge so that, since the history does not stand, the devil may be signified by Nabuchodonosor; which we do not accept, lest all that we read seem shadow and fables. For who does not know that madmen live like brute beasts in the fields and wooded places? And histories, Greek and Roman, relate that far more incredible things have happened to men, since fables also tell of Scylla and the chimera, the hydra and the centaurs, and many things of the kind; what wonder if, to show the power of God and to humble the pride of kings, Nabuchodonosor endured these things?

38_marg4488: Bede in the book On the Nature of Things. These words designate the incarnation of Christ, who fulfilled the law and the prophets, and was anointed “with the oil of gladness above his fellows”; the seventy weeks, divided by sevens of years, signify four hundred and ninety lunar years. But it must be noted that he declares these same weeks to be not simply reckoned but shortened, secretly warning us to know that the years are indicated as shorter than usual. Know therefore, he says, and take notice: “from the going forth of the word, to build up Jerusalem again, unto Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: and the street shall be built again, and the walls in straitness of times.” From Esdras’s narrative we have learned that Nehemias, cupbearer of King Artaxerxes, in the twentieth year of his reign, in the month of Nisan, obtained from him leave to restore the walls of Jerusalem, the temple having been built long before with Cyrus permitting. And that he completed this work also, as was said, in straitness of time, being so attacked by the neighboring nations that the builders, each with a sword girded at his side, are said to have fought with one hand and recovered the wall with the other. From this time, therefore, to Christ the prince seventy weeks are reckoned, that is, four hundred and ninety years of twelve lunar months, which are four hundred and seventy-five solar years. For the Persians reigned from the aforesaid twentieth year of King Artaxerxes to the death of Darius one hundred and eighteen years. From then the Macedonians, to the death of Cleopatra, three hundred years. Then the Romans held the monarchy until the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, fifty-seven years; which together, as we said, are four hundred and seventy-five solar years. And they are contained in twenty-five nineteen-year cycles. For nineteen times twenty-five makes four hundred and seventy-five. And because in each cycle seven embolismic months are added, multiply twenty-five by seven and it makes one hundred and seventy-five, which are the embolismic months of four hundred and seventy-five years. If therefore you wish to know how many lunar years these months make, divide the one hundred and seventy-five months by twelve, and they make fourteen years and seven months. Join these to the aforesaid four hundred and seventy-five years: there will be four hundred and eighty-nine years and seven months. And add these surplus months to part of the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, under whom the Lord suffered, and you will find the weeks fixed beforehand, or the term fixed beforehand, that is, from the going forth of the word by which it was commanded that the walls of Jerusalem be rebuilt, to his passion, seventy shortened weeks, that is, four hundred and ninety lunar years. And that by his baptism, when the saint of saints was anointed, the Holy Spirit descending upon him like a dove, not only the seven and sixty-two weeks had been completed, but also a part of the seventieth week was already begun. And after sixty-two weeks, he says, Christ shall be slain, and the people that shall deny him shall not be his. Christ was slain not immediately after the sixty-two and seven weeks, but at the end of the seventieth week, which, as far as we can judge, he set apart from the other weeks because he was to relate more about it. For in that week Christ was crucified, and was denied by the faithless people not only in the passion but continually from the time he began to be preached by John. But what follows: “And a people with their leader that shall come, shall destroy the city and the sanctuary: and the end thereof shall be waste, and after the end of the war the appointed desolation,” does not belong to the seventy weeks. For it had been foretold that the weeks themselves would reach to the leadership of Christ, but Scripture, having foretold his coming and passion, shows what would also happen after this to the people who would not receive him. For it says the leader to come is Titus, who in the forty-second year after the Lord’s passion, with the Roman people, so destroyed the city and the sanctuary that there did not remain “a stone upon a stone.” Whence, having touched on these things by anticipation, it soon returns to expounding the event of the week which it had passed over. “And he shall confirm the covenant,” that is, of faith, “with many, in one week,” that is, the last one itself, in which either John the Baptist, or the Lord, or the apostles by preaching converted many to the faith. “And in the half of the week the victim and the sacrifice shall fail”: the half of this week was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when, Christ’s baptism having begun, the purification by victims gradually began to grow cheap to the faithful. Again, what follows: “And there shall be in the temple the abomination of desolation: and the desolation shall continue even to the consummation, and to the end,” looks to later times, the truth of which prophecy is attested by the history of the ancients and the events of our own times.
